## Geoglyphs and the Andean Candelabra: What to See on the Nazca Plateau, Peru

### The Nazca Lines — One of Earth's Greatest Mysteries!

The Nazca Lines on the Nazca Plateau are among the most mysterious places on Earth. These enormous drawings, created by unknown artists in the desert, can be seen in their entirety only from a bird's-eye view. The gigantic geometric figures depict triangles, spirals, lines and constellations, as well as a monkey, spider, flowers, an astronaut and a hummingbird whose wingspan exceeds two hundred metres. They were created between the 1st and 5th centuries AD.

The Nazca Lines were first noticed in 1939 by the American archaeologist Paul Kosok as he flew over the plateau. Such patterns could not be identified from the ground; even today, the figures can only be made out from the air. Around thirty drawings, 788 different geometric figures — including trapezoids, triangles and spirals — and thousands of lines and strips can be found across the Nazca Plateau. In 1994, the geoglyphs were added to the UNESCO World Heritage List.

## Feel the Spirit of Peru!

A motorboat will take you to the Ballestas Islands, home to rare marine animals and birds. On the way, you will see the famous, mysterious "Candelabra", a gigantic figure carved into the rock by priests in ancient times. The Andean Candelabra, also known as the Paracas Candelabra, is a massive geoglyph on the slope of an enormous sandy hill in a Pacific Ocean bay on the Paracas Peninsula. The figure stretches 128 metres in length and almost 100 metres in width; its lines are between 0.5 and 4 metres thick and up to 2 metres deep. Its shape really does resemble a giant candlestick holding three candles, clearly visible both from the air and from the sea. This is a place to immerse yourself in Peru's mysterious atmosphere.

Livingston is one of the South Shetland Islands, located between Snow Island and Greenwich Island. Snow and ice cover most of the island. Rocky stretches of coastline provide places where marine animals come ashore.

On the southern coast lies Hannah Point, known for its penguin colonies and elephant seal haul-outs. Glacier-covered slopes and dark rocks at the water's edge are visible from the sea. Expedition landings depend on sea conditions and access to the shore.

### Livingston, a Small Town on the Río Dulce

Livingston is a colourful little town full of coconut groves, brightly painted wooden buildings, reggae music drifting from every direction and a fishing-based economy. Known for its distinctive blend of Guatemalan and Caribbean cultures, it stands at the mouth of the Río Dulce in the far northeast of Guatemala.

The Garifuna people who inhabit this area are descended from Africans who were enslaved and brought from the African continent to work on plantations, and from local Indigenous peoples. This meeting of communities gave rise to a distinctive culture and language. The town was named after the American legislator Edward Livingston, whose ideas were adopted by Guatemalan liberals in the early 19th century. Today, Livingston is a quiet, relaxed harbour, with small boats all around and a peaceful atmosphere.

## Relaxing in Livingston

### Livingston — A Blend of Cultures!

In Livingston, visitors can find everything they need — hotels, restaurants, banks and shops — along the main street. It runs from the Municipal Dock through the town and ends at the beach. Livingston is also the departure point for boat trips along the Río Quechuche and Río Cocolí, to the canyons of the Río Dulce, the abandoned town of Río Dulce (Fronteras), the 16th-century San Felipe Fortress, Lake Los Duarte, the ruins of Quiriguá, the Las Siete Altares waterfalls, and the protected beaches and reefs of the Sapodilla Cayes. It is also one of the region's best locations for sea fishing.
